vignette: Mahesh, a 35-year-old accountant of South-Eastern Asian heritage, had spent the last decade navigating the quiet rhythm of a suburban office, crunching numbers and balancing ledgers while his home life had frayed into a divorce that left him alone in a small apartment. Yet his daily routine was pierced by moments of sudden terror. The most unsettling of these were the intrusive memories that would flare up without warning, like an old film looping in his mind. One afternoon, while sorting tax returns, a sharp clack of a distant alarm sounded, and the image of a makeshift electric chair, hands pressed around his shoulders, flooded his awareness. The shock was not a physical alarm, but a mental one that made him freeze, the weight of that memory pressing down on his chest. He felt a rising sense of dread-fear of harm-that he could never quite shake, a belief that someone, anywhere, could still decide to inflict that same violence upon him. In that instant the intrusive memory acted as a trigger that, as he later understood, sent a wave of negative appraisals through his mind. The terror of that single event cascaded into a conviction that he could never be safe, and that whatever might happen would strike without warning. The same pattern appeared whenever he found himself speaking about the future or meeting strangers. In a quarterly planning session, as his supervisor asked him to outline next year's projections, he could not focus on the spreadsheet. The words "future" in the discussion activated a flood of images from the days of interrogation: the rusted steel walls, the cold breath of captors, the sense that each new calculation was an act of survival. He was certain that if he tried to map a future, he would be reminded of how uncertain and fragile that path could be. Similarly, when a new client approached the office for a consultation, the stranger's voice became a trigger that sent a jolt through his chest. The sudden surge of panic was not only a symptom; it was the catalyst that confirmed his growing belief that he could never know who might harm him or when. The connection between these triggers and the negative appraisals is clear in the way that the mere presence of an intrusive memory or a conversation about the future immediately provoked the same fear, a cycle that left him feeling perpetually exposed. These negative appraisals, in turn, reshaped the memories of that brutal period. Mahesh reported that the memory of the torture felt alien, as if it belonged to someone else rather than to himself. He could not place the moments in a coherent order; the sequence of electric shocks, the beating of his heart, the whispers of his captors, were all jumbled together, each fragment slipping through his consciousness. He described the experience as a film that played over and over again, each time the scenes blurred, the actors changed, and the climax remained undefined. The sense that he had been permanently damaged-an enduring change that had made him less capable, less sane-was the emotional core that drove this alien quality. His belief that others could have stopped the ordeal and that he could not have prevented it further solidified his view that the event had irrevocably altered him. The negative appraisals thus did not merely label the trauma; they actively shaped the content and form of the memory itself, making it feel detached and repetitive, as if a foreign narrative was being replayed. The day-to-day consequences of this loop have become pronounced. At work, he avoids planning sessions or meetings with unfamiliar colleagues, preferring the safety of routine tasks that do not involve future speculation or new interactions. The avoidance has begun to erode his career, with supervisors noting his reluctance to take on projects that require outreach or strategic vision. His relationships with friends have frayed; he no longer invites them for dinner, fearing that the conversation will spiral into topics he cannot control. At home, he spends long hours in front of the television, hoping that the background noise will drown the intrusive images that surface at random. The isolation has pushed him toward the decision to seek professional help. The most recent flashback, triggered by a mundane grocery run, left him shaking, convinced that the world was still a dangerous place, and that he had become a permanent victim of his past. He now fears that without intervention his sense of safety will continue to collapse, and he hopes that therapy can break the cycle between the triggers, the harmful beliefs, and the haunted memories that have hijacked his present.
